paras: The threatened lynching of William Robinson took place in Kanawha County, West Virginia, in November 1881, after Robinson was accused of shooting and killing Allen Belcher, the town marshal of Malden, on November 15. Telegraphic reports said a mob was coming or organizing to take Robinson from the Charleston jail and hang him, and guards, militia and federal marshals were posted around the jail. No attack on the jail was reported, and a Charleston correspondent wrote that no lynching had ever been planned.

Malden lay six miles above Charleston on the Kanawha River. According to the Wheeling Register's Charleston correspondent, Belcher, a former justice of the district, had served for some time as marshal and had tried to suppress "a few roughs" in the town. The same writer described Robinson as "a drunken ruffian, the terror of the whole village," who was said to have recently shot at Henry Spriegel and attacked John Brown with a knife, and who had been released on bail a few weeks before.

On Tuesday, November 15, Robinson was reported to have gone to Malden, defied the authorities and threatened to kill Belcher if the marshal interfered with him. When Belcher tried to arrest him, Robinson was said to have shot him through the heart, killing him instantly, and to have fired at the mayor, D. H. Putney, without hitting him. Robinson was arrested and taken to the jail at Charleston.

A Charleston telegram of November 16 said that "some fears" were entertained of another "court of Judge Lynch." A report printed on November 18 said lynching was "freely talked of," that a mob was said to be coming from Malden to take Robinson from the jail and hang him, and that Colonel Appleton had ordered the Hale Riflemen to be ready to protect the jail. A Charleston dispatch of November 19 placed the supposed mob on Campbell's Creek instead and said the United States Marshal at Hinton was guarding the jail. As late as November 25 a Romney paper reported that U.S. deputy marshals were still guarding the jail to keep Robinson from being lynched.

No attack on the jail, and no one hurt in connection with the threat, appears in any report. The Register's correspondent wrote that after thirty-six hours of guard duty it was learned that no mob was organizing, and the guards were withdrawn. No report of an indictment or trial of Robinson was found in the coverage.

Coverage came entirely from white newspapers, beginning with a special telegram to the Richmond Dispatch under the headline "A West Virginia Tragedy." Papers outside the state played up the danger, with headlines such as "A Murderer's Life in Danger" and, in the Chicago Tribune, "A Strong Desire to Lynch." A syndicated crime column printed in Dakota and Wisconsin weeklies on November 24 and 25 went further than any other report, stating that "A mob collected to lynch the murderer."

West Virginia papers were more measured. The Wheeling Intelligencer ran the threat under "The Kanawha Troubles" beside news of state troops at Coal Valley, and the South Branch Intelligencer said those troops were stationed at the mines, which suggests a separate disturbance. The Wheeling Register's correspondent, under the headline "Atrocious Murder—Threats of Lynching," ridiculed the precautions as "preposterous" and a "pompous farce," mocking the old gatling gun wheeled into position and the scouts sent out to find the expected mob. All the papers called Robinson a "desperado," a "notorious character" or a "murderer," and none described him by race. A Putnam Democrat item reprinted in Philippi in December mentioned only the killing and blamed it on whisky.

Reports disagree on whether a mob ever existed. The early reports spoke of a mob "reported" coming from Malden or "supposed to be organizing" on Campbell's Creek, the syndicated column said a mob "collected," and the Register's Charleston correspondent, the only local eyewitness account of the jail guard, said no lynching had been contemplated and no one had suggested violence. Accounts also differ on whether Robinson fired at the mayor twice or three times, and on whether the shooting took place in the afternoon or the evening.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Robinson
bases: Reports that a mob was coming or organizing to take Robinson from the Charleston jail and hang him, and the guard posted against it (A2, A4, A10), make this a threatened lynching; no one was hurt.
Robinson was not killed; he remained under guard in the Charleston jail (A10), and the existence of the mob itself is contested (A5).
Independent dispatches report the lynching threat and the jail guard (A1, A2, A4, A10), but the Register's Charleston correspondent says no lynching was ever contemplated and no mob organized (A5).

Syndicated crime column called Robinson 'a desperado' and reported the mob as fact.
The Wheeling Register's letter called the killing 'atrocious' and Robinson 'a drunken ruffian' while mocking the anti-lynching precautions as a 'pompous farce'.
